title: How the Peace Corps Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Peace Corps: its origins in John F. Kennedy's 1960 University of Michigan speech and San Francisco Cow Palace speech, the March 1, 1961 executive order, and its later move to an independent agency under Jimmy Carter. They cover its funding, the three-part mission statement, the application and interview process, eligibility rules (no pets, no children, married couples), the 27-month service term, packing limits, living conditions, day-to-day work, the readjustment allowance and hiring priority after service, measuring success, and criticisms including sexual assault reporting, the murders of Kate Puzey and Deborah Gardner, and alleged CIA intelligence ties in Bolivia. The episode ends with listener mail from an Irish listener about the terrorist watch list episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode dedication
segments.summary: Hosts joke about recording setup and tape supplies, then dedicate the episode to Peace Corps volunteers who have written in over the years.

segments.title: Origins of the Peace Corps
segments.summary: Kennedy's October 1960 University of Michigan speech and Cow Palace speech, the 25,000 letters, the March 1, 1961 executive order, the budget enactment, and Nixon and Carter's later changes making it an independent agency.

segments.title: Funding, directors, and countries served
segments.summary: Discussion of the Peace Corps budget (about four hundred million dollars), presidential expansion pushes, past directors, and the countries served including the first two, Tanganyika and Ghana.

segments.title: Mission statement and purpose
segments.summary: The three-part mission statement and how it differs from other foreign aid, with the point that host countries sometimes do not realize it is a U.S. government program.

segments.title: Application and eligibility
segments.summary: The 27-month commitment, the living allowance, the six thousand dollar readjustment payment, the extensive online application covering background, drinking, finances and references, and rules on age, diplomas, marriage, children and pets.

segments.title: Interview, invitation, and assignment
segments.summary: The interview screening for completion of service, sample interview questions, the ten-day invitation decision, placement based on skills and languages, and the three-month training period.

segments.title: Packing, living conditions, and day-to-day life
segments.summary: The eighty-pound, two-bag packing limit, electricity and water realities, the freedom volunteers have day to day, friends visiting, packages, and a former director's concern about volunteers treating it as a spring break.

segments.title: Benefits after service and measuring success
segments.summary: Resume value and hiring priority for government jobs after service, and the difficulty of measuring the mission's success, with volunteers reporting personal gains.

segments.title: Criticisms: crime, murders, and CIA allegations
segments.summary: Sexual assault reporting problems and the First Response Action group, the five-year staff limit, the murders of Kate Puzey in Benin and Deborah Gardner in Tonga, and the 2008 Bolivia allegations about intelligence reporting.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank Peace Corps volunteers and point listeners to the search bar for more.

segments.title: Listener mail from Ireland
segments.summary: An Irish listener recounts panicking over the terrorist watch list episode while driving in Dublin, and shout-outs to members of the Irish Battalion.
